description: Golden regression set for DPNP - Data Parallel Extension for NumPy
version_or_doc_snapshot: dpnp 0.17.0 documentation (intelpython.github.io/dpnp, accessed 2026-06-10) and IntelPython/dpnp GitHub repository issues

questions.text: Scenario: You replace numpy.unique(arr, sorted=False) with dpnp.unique(arr, sorted=False) in production code and get TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'sorted'. This breaks your data pipeline. According to dpnp documentation, how should you check API compatibility before migration, and what's the recommended fallback pattern for unsupported parameters?
expected_topics: dpnp implements a subset of NumPy - not all parameters supported even when function exists
the API reference lists supported functions but parameter-level coverage requires checking documentation for each function
recommended pattern: try dpnp operation, catch NotImplementedError or TypeError, fall back to numpy using asnumpy() conversion
proactive checking: test critical code paths with dpnp before production deployment
no automated compatibility checker currently available - must test manually

metadata.why_it_matters: This is a top-3 migration blocker. Users assume 'drop-in replacement' means full API parity, leading to production failures.

questions.text: Scenario: Your dpnp code works on your workstation with GPU but crashes on a cloud VM with 'Default device is unavailable'. You realize dpnp was trying to use GPU. According to dpnp documentation, how do you (a) check which device dpnp will use, (b) explicitly select CPU, and (c) handle environments where GPU is unavailable?
expected_topics: dpnp allocates memory on 'default SYCL device' - GPU if available, otherwise host CPU
check device: use dpctl.select_default_device() or inspect array.sycl_device property
force CPU: set device context using dpctl.device_context('cpu') or equivalent
graceful fallback: catch device errors and fall back to NumPy or explicitly use CPU device
environment-dependent behavior means code may work in development but fail in production

metadata.why_it_matters: Cloud/container deployments frequently have no GPU. Silent device selection breaks portability.

questions.text: Scenario: You've migrated 80% of your NumPy code to dpnp successfully. Then at runtime in production, you hit NotImplementedError for a function you didn't test. According to dpnp documentation, what's the recommended strategy for (a) discovering unsupported APIs before deployment, (b) handling NotImplementedError gracefully, and (c) mixing dpnp and NumPy code safely?
expected_topics: dpnp implements a subset of NumPy - comprehensive testing required before production
no static analysis tool to check compatibility - must test code paths
graceful handling pattern: try dpnp operation, catch NotImplementedError, fall back to numpy using asnumpy()
mixing dpnp and numpy is safe but has conversion cost - avoid repeated conversions in tight loops
incremental migration recommended: start with hot paths, keep fallback to numpy for edge cases

metadata.why_it_matters: Runtime errors in production are costly. Documentation must provide proactive testing strategy.

questions.text: Scenario: You need to checkpoint your ML model which includes dpnp arrays, but pickle.dump() or numpy.save() fails. According to dpnp documentation, what's the recommended approach for persisting dpnp arrays, and what's the trade-off?
expected_topics: dpnp arrays are not directly serializable due to SYCL device memory
recommended pattern: convert to NumPy with asnumpy() before saving, convert back to dpnp after loading
trade-off: serialization involves device-to-host copy, adding overhead
for frequent checkpointing, consider keeping NumPy copies or using device-aware serialization if available
this limitation affects model saving, distributed training, and any pipeline with persistence

metadata.why_it_matters: Checkpointing is critical for long-running training. Silent failure breaks workflows.

questions.text: Scenario: You replaced numpy with dpnp in a data preprocessing pipeline expecting automatic speedup. For small arrays (100-1000 elements) processed in tight loops, the code is now slower. The documentation says dpnp is 'optimized for data parallel devices' but doesn't specify when it's faster. What guidance should dpnp documentation provide about array sizes, overhead, and when NOT to use dpnp?
expected_topics: dpnp has kernel dispatch and device memory overhead that can dominate for small operations
general rule: larger arrays (typically >10,000 elements) and math-heavy operations benefit most
tight loops with small arrays favor NumPy's lower overhead
first execution includes JIT compilation overhead - subsequent runs should be faster
selective adoption recommended: profile first, use dpnp for bottlenecks, keep NumPy for small-array hot paths

metadata.why_it_matters: Unrealistic expectations lead to disappointment and abandonment. Documentation must set accurate expectations about performance characteristics.

questions.text: Scenario: You run 'pip install dpnp' expecting it to work like other Python packages, but encounter installation failures because the Intel package index or native runtime dependencies are missing. According to dpnp documentation, what installation method is recommended, when is pip acceptable, and what dependencies are required?
expected_topics: conda installation via Intel channel is the recommended path for most users
pip installation is available as an alternative when using Intel's pip index and compatible native dependencies
dpnp requires SYCL runtime and Intel oneAPI components that conda handles more consistently
building from source requires oneAPI DPC++ compiler and specific oneAPI libraries
conda installation ensures compatible versions of all dependencies

metadata.why_it_matters: First installation failure creates high abandonment risk. Clear installation guidance prevents frustration.

questions.text: Scenario: You discover that dpnp.linalg.cholesky returns significantly different values than numpy.linalg.cholesky for the same input matrix (not just floating-point precision differences). According to dpnp best practices, how should you validate numerical correctness when migrating from NumPy, and what testing strategy ensures dpnp operations produce correct results?
expected_topics: dpnp aims for numerical equivalence with NumPy but bugs can cause differences
recommended practice: compare dpnp results against NumPy for critical operations during migration
use numpy.testing.assert_allclose() with appropriate tolerances to validate results
report significant discrepancies as bugs - they are not expected behavior
implement regression tests that compare dpnp vs NumPy outputs before production deployment
for mission-critical computations, consider dual-running dpnp and NumPy during validation phase

metadata.why_it_matters: Silent incorrect results are the most dangerous class of bugs. Testing strategy prevents production disasters.

questions.text: Scenario: You've migrated a large matrix multiplication workload from NumPy (which uses OpenBLAS) to dpnp expecting GPU speedup. For 5000×5000 matrices, NumPy takes 0.5s but dpnp takes 2.0s (slower!). According to dpnp documentation, what factors affect matrix multiplication performance, and what's the recommended approach to diagnose and fix slow linear algebra operations?
expected_topics: dpnp uses oneMKL as BLAS backend (CPU) or oneMKL for GPU
Small matrices may have kernel launch overhead on GPU
Data transfer overhead (host↔device) if not accounted for
Array must be on device before operation; check with array.sycl_device
Profiling recommendations: time data transfer separately, warmup runs for JIT compilation
Size threshold where GPU becomes faster (typically >1000×1000 for matmul)
Recommend: benchmark with data already on device, compare device-to-device computation only

metadata.why_it_matters: Matrix ops are core ML workload; unexpectedly slow performance blocks adoption

questions.text: Scenario: Your NumPy code uses numpy.linalg.solve() for linear systems and numpy.linalg.eig() for eigenvalues. When you replace with dpnp, solve() works but eig() raises NotImplementedError. According to dpnp documentation, how do you (a) check which linalg functions are supported before migration, (b) handle unsupported functions gracefully, and (c) mix dpnp and scipy.linalg when needed?
expected_topics: dpnp.linalg implements subset of numpy.linalg - not all functions available
Check API reference documentation for supported functions list
Recommended pattern: try dpnp operation, catch NotImplementedError, fallback to numpy/scipy
For scipy.linalg: must convert dpnp array to numpy with asnumpy(), incurs transfer cost
Alternative: use scipy.linalg directly with numpy arrays for unsupported operations
Future: API coverage expands over releases, check release notes

metadata.why_it_matters: Scientific computing relies heavily on linalg; API gaps break workflows

questions.text: Scenario: You're migrating signal processing code using numpy.fft.fft() on 1M-point signals. NumPy (using pocketfft) takes 50ms. With dpnp, the same operation takes 300ms (6x slower). According to dpnp documentation, what FFT backend does dpnp use, what factors affect FFT performance, and when should you expect speedup over NumPy?
expected_topics: dpnp uses oneMKL FFT backend for both CPU and GPU
First FFT call may include plan creation overhead (warmup effect)
Data transfer overhead if array not already on device
FFT performance depends on signal size (power-of-2 is optimal)
CPU FFT may be slower than optimized NumPy/SciPy backends for small signals
GPU FFT becomes faster for very large transforms (>1M points) or batch operations
Recommend: benchmark with pre-allocated device arrays, multiple runs for accurate timing

metadata.why_it_matters: Signal processing and ML (spectrogram features) depend on fast FFT

questions.text: Scenario: You set numpy.random.seed(42) in your training code for reproducibility. After migrating to dpnp, you set dpnp.random.seed(42) but get different random numbers than NumPy, breaking reproducibility. According to dpnp documentation, how does dpnp RNG work, can you get NumPy-equivalent random sequences, and how do you ensure reproducibility across CPU/GPU devices?
expected_topics: dpnp uses oneMKL RNG backend, different algorithm than NumPy
Same seed produces different sequences than NumPy (not a drop-in replacement for RNG)
Cannot replicate exact NumPy random sequences with dpnp
Reproducibility within dpnp: same seed + same device → same sequence
Reproducibility across devices (CPU/GPU): NOT guaranteed with same seed
Recommended: if exact NumPy sequences required, use numpy.random and convert arrays
For dpnp reproducibility: fix seed, document device used, version-pin dpnp/oneMKL

metadata.why_it_matters: ML training reproducibility is critical; unexpected RNG differences break experiments

questions.text: Scenario: Your dpnp code works on workstation with 16GB GPU but crashes with 'out of memory' on server with 8GB GPU. NumPy equivalent works fine (using CPU RAM). According to dpnp documentation, how do you (a) check GPU memory availability, (b) handle OOM errors gracefully, (c) control device memory usage, and (d) fall back to CPU when GPU memory insufficient?
expected_topics: dpnp allocates on default SYCL device (GPU if available), which has limited memory
No built-in memory limit or automatic CPU fallback on OOM
Check device memory: use dpctl to query device memory capacity
Handling OOM: catch runtime errors, fall back to NumPy or explicit CPU device
Control memory: explicitly use CPU device with dpctl.device_context('cpu')
Batch processing strategy: process data in chunks that fit in GPU memory
Alternative: keep large data in NumPy, selectively move chunks to dpnp for computation

metadata.why_it_matters: GPU memory constraints are common blocker; silent OOM crashes hurt production

questions.text: Scenario: You have ML pipeline using PyTorch for neural network and NumPy for preprocessing. You want to accelerate preprocessing with dpnp but need to pass results to PyTorch tensors efficiently. According to dpnp documentation, can you convert dpnp arrays to PyTorch tensors zero-copy, or must you transfer through NumPy (slow)?
expected_topics: dpnp arrays are not directly compatible with PyTorch (no zero-copy conversion)
Must convert: dpnp array → numpy (with asnumpy()) → pytorch tensor
This involves device-to-host copy (GPU to CPU) then potentially CPU to GPU for PyTorch
Double transfer overhead makes this inefficient for GPU-to-GPU workflow
Alternative: if dpnp uses Intel GPU and PyTorch uses NVIDIA GPU, must transfer anyway
Workaround: use DLPack protocol if supported (check dpnp/PyTorch versions)
Recommendation: evaluate if dpnp preprocessing overhead offset by transfer cost

metadata.why_it_matters: ML pipelines mix frameworks; transfer overhead can negate acceleration benefits

questions.text: Scenario: You pass dpnp arrays to scikit-learn's fit() method expecting it to work (since it accepts 'array-like'). Instead you get 'expected numpy array' errors or crashes. According to dpnp documentation, does dpnp implement the NumPy array protocol for scikit-learn compatibility, and what's the recommended pattern for using dpnp with scikit-learn?
expected_topics: scikit-learn expects NumPy arrays or objects implementing NumPy array protocol
dpnp arrays may not fully implement protocol (check __array__ method support)
Most reliable pattern: convert dpnp to numpy before passing to scikit-learn
Use asnumpy() to convert: clf.fit(X_dpnp.asnumpy(), y_dpnp.asnumpy())
This incurs device-to-host transfer cost, limiting acceleration benefits
Alternative: use Intel Extension for Scikit-learn (sklearnex) which may have dpnp support
Recommendation: accelerate data preprocessing with dpnp, convert before ML model

metadata.why_it_matters: Scikit-learn is ubiquitous in ML; incompatibility blocks adoption

questions.text: Scenario: Your NumPy code uses boolean indexing: arr[arr > 0]. After migrating to dpnp, the operation is very slow compared to NumPy for large arrays. According to dpnp documentation, how does dpnp implement advanced indexing (fancy indexing, boolean masks), and what performance characteristics should you expect?
expected_topics: dpnp supports boolean and integer array indexing (fancy indexing)
Performance may differ from NumPy due to device kernel dispatch overhead
Boolean indexing creates a copy, not a view (same as NumPy)
Large boolean masks on GPU may have overhead for small result arrays
Recommend: if indexing result is small, consider numpy for that operation
Batch boolean indexing operations when possible to amortize kernel launch

metadata.why_it_matters: Data filtering with boolean masks is extremely common in data science

questions.text: Scenario: Your NumPy code relies on reshape() returning a view (zero-copy) for performance. After migrating to dpnp, you're unsure if dpnp.reshape() creates views or copies. According to dpnp documentation, which array operations return views vs copies, and how does this compare to NumPy?
expected_topics: dpnp follows NumPy semantics: reshape() returns view when possible, copy otherwise
View vs copy depends on memory layout (C-contiguous vs Fortran-contiguous)
Transpose always returns view (same as NumPy)
Check if operation returned view: compare array.base attribute
Performance implication: copies involve memory allocation and data transfer on device
Recommend: test view behavior for critical paths, avoid unnecessary copies

metadata.why_it_matters: View semantics critical for performance; copies can negate acceleration

questions.text: Scenario: You have large datasets stored as NumPy .npz files. You want to load them directly into dpnp arrays to avoid CPU→GPU transfer. According to dpnp documentation, can you load .npy/.npz files directly into dpnp device memory, or must you load with numpy.load() then convert?
expected_topics: dpnp does not have native .npy/.npz loader (as of current version)
Must use numpy.load() to load files, then convert to dpnp with dpnp.array()
Conversion involves host-to-device transfer (CPU to GPU)
For large files, this adds I/O overhead + transfer overhead
Workaround: load in chunks if memory limited
Alternative: use memory-mapped arrays (numpy.memmap) for partial loading
Future: watch for direct device I/O support in future dpnp versions

metadata.why_it_matters: Data loading is entry point; slow loading hurts adoption

questions.text: Scenario: Your NumPy code uses structured arrays (dtype with named fields) for heterogeneous data: np.dtype([('x', 'f8'), ('y', 'i4')]). After migrating to dpnp, you get NotImplementedError. According to dpnp documentation, does dpnp support structured dtypes, and what's the workaround?
expected_topics: dpnp does not support structured dtypes (as of current version)
Limitation inherited from GPU computing constraints (non-contiguous layouts)
Workaround: split structured array into separate arrays per field
Alternative: keep structured data in NumPy, convert individual fields to dpnp as needed
Performance trade-off: separate arrays may be more efficient on GPU anyway
Recommendation: restructure data as dict of arrays rather than structured array

metadata.why_it_matters: Scientific data often uses structured arrays; incompatibility breaks pipelines

questions.text: Scenario: Your NumPy code computes column-wise sums: arr.sum(axis=0). After migrating to dpnp, the result shape is correct but performance is slower than expected for large arrays. According to dpnp documentation, how are axis-based reductions implemented, and when should you expect performance improvement over NumPy?
expected_topics: dpnp implements axis-based reductions (sum, mean, std, min, max) similar to NumPy
GPU reductions are efficient for large arrays and specific patterns (full reduction best)
Partial reductions (along axis) may have overhead due to memory access patterns
Small arrays or unusual axis orders may be slower than NumPy CPU implementation
Recommend: benchmark full reductions first (axis=None) vs partial reductions
Batch multiple reductions when possible to amortize kernel launch overhead

metadata.why_it_matters: Statistical operations are extremely common; poor performance hurts adoption

questions.text: Scenario: You have existing CuPy code running on NVIDIA GPUs. Your team is evaluating Intel GPUs and dpnp as alternative. According to dpnp documentation, what are the main API and behavior differences between CuPy and dpnp that will require code changes during migration?
expected_topics: Device management: CuPy uses CUDA device model, dpnp uses SYCL/dpctl
Device selection: cupy.cuda.Device(0) vs dpctl.device_context('gpu:0')
Memory management: cupy.get_default_memory_pool() vs dpctl memory (different APIs)
Kernel customization: CuPy supports custom CUDA kernels, dpnp uses SYCL (different)
API coverage: some CuPy functions may not exist in dpnp (check documentation)
Synchronization: cupy.cuda.Stream vs dpctl queue semantics
Performance tuning: different architecture (NVIDIA vs Intel GPU) needs different tuning

metadata.why_it_matters: CuPy users are natural migration candidates; need clear migration path
